analysis.one_liner: Levy a small tax on stock, bond, derivative, and digital asset trades to fund public investments.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a small tax on the transfer of stocks, bonds, derivatives, and digital assets: 0.5% of the value of a stock trade, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives. The tax is collected by exchanges and brokers, with exceptions for initial stock offerings, very short-term debt, and routine securities lending. Households earning under $50,000 ($75,000 for joint filers) would get a credit refunding any of the tax they pay, so ordinary small savers would be shielded. Revenue would go to public investments; the bill names families, communities, infrastructure, and the environment.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday taxpayers benefit twice over: the bill explicitly gives a full credit to individuals earning under $50,000 (or $75,000 for couples) that refunds any trade tax they pay, so low- and middle-income savers pay nothing, while the revenue collected from high-volume trading would be available for public investments in families, communities, infrastructure, and the environment. The bill's stated purpose also includes reducing market volatility, which its supporters link to high-frequency speculative trading.

how_it_helps.text: The tax is 0.5% on stock and other equity transfers, 0.1% on debt securities, and 0.005% on derivatives, so a $10,000 stock trade would carry a $50 tax — a cost borne mainly by high-volume traders and large institutional investors.

Individuals with modified adjusted gross income at or below $50,000 ($75,000 for joint filers) can claim a tax credit equal to the full amount of trade tax they paid, meaning ordinary savers in that income range are made whole.
The bill states its purpose as investing in families, communities, infrastructure, and the environment, strengthening financial security, expanding opportunity, and reducing market volatility.

analysis.who_pays: Frequent and high-volume traders pay directly: exchanges and brokers must collect the tax on trades they clear or execute, and Wall Street firms, hedge funds, high-frequency trading shops, and digital-asset platforms bear most of it. Some costs can be passed to larger investors and, to a limited degree, retirement accounts and mutual fund shareholders above the income threshold, since the credit only refunds the tax for households under $50,000/$75,000.

drawbacks.text: Traders above the income-credit threshold — including pension funds, 401(k) investors with higher incomes, and mutual fund holders — would bear the tax without any offset, since the refund credit only covers individuals under $50,000 ($75,000 joint), and economists debate how much of a transaction tax gets passed through to investors in fees and trading costs.

The bill exempts initial stock and bond issues but taxes every resale, and a similar tax could encourage trading to move to foreign venues or shift into exempted instruments, shrinking expected revenue — a concern the bill addresses only through broad Secretary authority to write anti-avoidance regulations.

The tax applies to every transfer of ownership in stocks, bonds, derivatives, and digital assets, including routine rebalancing by mutual funds and ETFs, which critics say could raise costs inside retirement vehicles even where the underlying purpose is to tax speculation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is aimed squarely at large, frequent traders: rates are small in absolute terms, initial capital-raising is exempt, and a full credit shields households under $50,000/$75,000 from any net cost. The main honest concerns are leakage of trading to untaxed venues or exempted instruments (which would reduce revenue), and the absence of any credit for investors above the income threshold, including some retirement savers. On balance the bill concentrates its cost on high-volume financial trading while directing the proceeds to public investment.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2023 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2025 without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Tax on Wall Street Speculation Act on June 14, 2023, joined by Senator Alex Padilla, making two senators in total.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, and no further action appears in the complete action history.

Only one senator cosponsored the bill, and the Finance Committee never reported it, held it for a vote, or scheduled it; the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, leaving the bill dead without ever reaching the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-volume Wall Street trading firms, exchanges, and large institutional investors are better off because the tax never advanced: they keep trading without the new 0.5% (stocks), 0.1% (bonds), and 0.005% (derivatives) levy, and no new revenue was created for public investment.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street trading firms and exchanges

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it, keeping it off the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the party split was never tested; the bill's only recorded support came from one independent and one Democrat, and no senator is recorded as opposing it directly.

industries.note: They are the designated collectors of the new tax on every covered trade they execute or clear, adding a compliance and cost burden that would fall heaviest on high-volume operations. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the public interest in the revenue and low-income credit it offered.

These firms execute enormous numbers of transactions, so even a 0.005%–0.5% rate on each trade would aggregate into a substantial annual cost, which is the bill's intended target. The bill's framing ties the tax to curbing volatility from rapid speculation.

industries.industry: Institutional investors and retirement fund managers
industries.note: Every purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives by mutual funds, ETFs, and pension portfolios would carry the tax, with no refund credit for holders above $50,000/$75,000 in income, raising costs inside widely held funds. Offsetting that, the bill exempts securities lending arrangements that are central to fund operations.

industries.industry: Digital asset and crypto trading platforms
industries.note: Digital assets are expressly covered at the 0.5% rate, so crypto exchanges and their high-turnover customers would face the tax on every transfer of ownership. The industry's interest lay in avoiding the tax, which would have funded public goods other taxpayers benefit from.

Initial issuances of stocks, bonds, and digital assets are explicitly exempt, so the tax does not apply when a company first sells securities to investors. This spares the cost of raising new capital from new issues.
